rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L08.html section 5 (line 272): containment, monotone expected maximum, and the null-win statement
rows.evidence: Re-derived. Let Q_N be the maximum of N null statistics and X_N the new null. Q_N = max(Q_(N-1), X_N) >= Q_(N-1) pointwise, for any joint law of the statistics. (a) E[Q_N] >= E[Q_(N-1)]: the expected maximum cannot fall as N grows. (b) {Z + delta > Q_N} is a subset of {Z + delta > Q_(N-1)}, so the probability that the genuine configuration wins cannot rise (containment, the T span that was already at 584f614). (c) The complement: P(some null beats the genuine) = 1 - P(genuine wins) cannot fall, so 'the null configurations win at least as often' (T). Bound: Lesson 1 Theorem 2.1 (L01.html line 82) states 'Let Z_1, ..., Z_N each have the standard normal distribution, with any joint distribution, and N >= 2. Then E[max Z_n] <= sqrt(2 ln N)'; its proof (Jensen, e^(lambda E M) <= sum E e^(lambda Z_n) = N e^(lambda^2/2), then lambda = sqrt(2 ln N)) is re-derived and holds with no independence. Numerical spot check (scratch scripts/l08_sec5_monotone.py, seed 777, 60,000 draws, N up to 60; output out_l08_sec5_monotone.txt): E[max] of the first N is non-decreasing in N for an equicorrelated law (rho 0.9), independent normals, a comonotone law and a block-random law; at every N it lies below sqrt(2 ln N) (smallest margins 0.9973, 0.5416, 1.1820 and 0.5990); P(genuine wins) with k nulls, k = 1..39, is non-increasing (0.8778, 0.8185, 0.7111, 0.6612, 0.5417, ... ). All checks pass.

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Remark 2.9 (lines 204-206): the normal-law mean, the pass probability 1/2, the median PSR, and T_beta
rows.evidence: Re-derived from the 8352c53 text. (i) Z_T is approximately N(mu, sd^2) with mu = (SR - SR*) sqrt(T-1)/sqrt(b) (Theorem 1.2 with the plug-in bracket). At T = MinTRL computed from the true values, MinTRL = 1 + b (z/(SR - SR*))^2 (Proposition 2.6(i)), so mu^2 = (SR - SR*)^2 (MinTRL - 1)/b = z^2 and mu = z for a positive margin. (ii) P(Z >= z) = 1 - Phi((z - mu)/sd) = 1/2 for every sd > 0 when mu = z, since a normal law's median is its mean. (iii) The median PSR is Phi(median Z) = Phi(z) = 1 - alpha. (iv) With sd 1 and mu = z + z_(1-beta), P(Z >= z) = Phi(z_(1-beta)) = 1 - beta, so T_beta = 1 + b ((z + z_(1-beta))/(SR - SR*))^2. Numerical spot check (scratch scripts/l07_remark29.py, output out_l07_remark29.txt, scipy): z_0.95 = 1.644854, z_0.80 = 0.841621; P(Z >= z | mu = z) = 0.5000 at sd 0.5, 0.911, 1.0 and 1.5; median PSR at MinTRL = 0.950000. For SR 0.09 and skew -2, kurtosis 9: b = 1.1962; MinTRL = 400.5520, ceiling 401; T_beta = 914.0339, ceiling 915; mean at 401 equals z exactly (1.644854). The sd statement ('close to 1 when the margin is small') is the first-order result sd = 1 - SR b'(SR)/(2b) = 0.9112 at SR 0.09 (Lab 4 interpretation), so it is a small-margin statement, consistent with the Remark. The statements are correct as conditional on the normal law (T). The unmarked finite-record sentence is handled by L07-grade-remark2.9-about-half (FAIL).

rows.evidence: unchanged since 584f614 (git diff checked); round-13 evidence: Re-checked. The back now says only what Proposition 5.4 proves: "It uses V1 + V2 instead of theta. For jointly normal returns with a common per-period Sharpe ratio SR and SR^2 < 2 (Proposition 5.4) it is undersized under positive correlation and oversized under negative correlation. In general it is oversized exactly when theta > V1 + V2." Proposition 5.4 (line 426-428) gives the limit 2(1 - Phi(z sqrt((V1+V2)/theta))), which is below alpha when theta < V1+V2 and above when theta > V1+V2. Re-derived: Corollary 5.2 gives theta = 2(1-rho) + (SR1^2 + SR2^2)/2 - SR1 SR2 rho^2 and V_i = 1 + SR_i^2/2, so for a common SR, theta - (V1+V2) = -rho(2 + SR^2 rho), whose sign is -sign(rho) when SR^2 < 2 (since 2 + SR^2 rho >= 2 - SR^2 > 0). Monte Carlo (4e6 draws, scratch math_checks.py, math_checks_out.txt) confirms the closed form for theta to 0.0035 at the largest deviation across rho in {-0.9,...,0.9} and three SR pairs. No numbers on this card. T is correct. [8352c53: cards.json changed for S7-c154, S7-c161 and S7-c219 and gained S7-c223 (L07) and other units' cards; this card is unchanged (git diff checked).]

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/cards.json S7-c212 (L08, new, grade T); course/modules/S/S7/L08.html section 5; key-results row 858
rows.evidence: unchanged since 584f614 (git diff checked); round-13 evidence: Claim: adding a null trial cannot raise the probability that a genuine configuration wins in sample, whatever the joint law. Proof (re-derived): let X0 be the genuine in-sample statistic and M_k the maximum of k null statistics. The winning event with k nulls is {X0 > M_k}; adding a null Y gives {X0 > max(M_k, Y)}, which is contained in {X0 > M_k}, so its probability cannot exceed the earlier one. No independence or distributional assumption is used. Numerical spot check (scratch scripts/spot_checks.py, 400,000 draws, a common-factor joint law, N-1 = 0,1,4,9,39 nulls): the win probability is non-increasing at every size (for example 0.6448 -> 0.4817 when a second null is added, 0.0513 -> 0.0502 at 39 nulls). The card's back matches Section 5's text. Grade T is right (a proof on the page). PASS. rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Remark 2.9 (line 204): the sentence 'A finite record passes about half the time to the extent that the approximation holds.' (no claim span); and misconception 2 (line 566): 'Computed from a true Sharpe ratio, it is a break-even length at which the test passes about half the time'
rows.evidence: Re-checked from scratch against the 8352c53 text. (1) Unmarked: the sentence is a substantive finite-sample claim with no claim span (BUILDER_RULES 2.1). The 8352c53 edit wrapped the T statements in prose but left this sentence bare. (2) Support and grade: its only support on the page is Lab 4. The twin's output, digit for digit equal to the page (lab-S7-L07-4, out_cmp_L07_4.txt), gives 'MinTRL 401 0.9473 0.4888': 48.9% of 401-day records pass. Lab 4 simulates exponential shocks with skewness -2 and kurtosis 9, so every moment is finite; the simulation does not test the approximation for any tail index. The grade C with Lab 4 as basis is right for the claim. (3) Counter-evidence (BUILDER_RULES 5; VERIFIER 2.3). Kao, Lee and Lee (2025), Review of Quantitative Finance and Accounting 67(2) 869-889, doi 10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6, found by Crossref query 'Estimated Sharpe ratio of asset returns with fat tails' (Crossref record fetched 2026-10-20; abstract read on the publisher page link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6). Abstract, quoted: 'We show that the asymptotic behavior of the estimated Sharpe ratio is biased and converges at a slower rate as 2 < kappa < 4 ... It is also shown that the asymptotic unbiasedness and normality of the estimated Sharpe ratio can only be established as asset returns have a finite (4 + epsilon)th moment with epsilon >= 0, i.e., kappa > 4.' This contests the normal approximation on which the sentence rests, for tail indexes between 2 and 4, and the page does not say so: Remark 2.9 gives no fourth-moment condition beyond 'By Theorem 1.2', and section 6 (line 531) says only that for heavy-tailed returns 'the plug-in standard error is itself unreliable'. The same paper's point appears in Choufani (2026), SSRN 10.2139/ssrn.7024958 (Crossref abstract read), a working paper that makes the same point for MinTRL. The Remark's T statements are conditional on Theorem 1.2, whose statement assumes E[r^4] < infinity, so they are not contested; the bare C sentence and misconception 2 are one-sided. Search record: Crossref bibliographic queries 'Estimated Sharpe ratio fat tails', 'Minimum Track Record Length Under Fat Tails', 'Sharpe ratio infinite fourth moment central limit theorem stable', 'Sharpe ratio finite-sample bias'; OpenCitations not needed. kao2025 is not in references/references.json: add_reference.py --dry-run with the citation string in the fix returns WOULD ADD (scratch dryrun_kao.out).

rows.location: course/modules/S/S7/L07.html Corollary 5.2 (line 405-410), Proposition 5.4 (line 425-431), key-results rows 747-748
rows.evidence: unchanged since 584f614 (git diff checked); round-13 evidence: New row; re-derived and spot-checked numerically (scratch math_checks.py, output math_checks_out.txt). Influence of the Sharpe estimator for standardized return u: psi = u - (SR/2)(u^2 - 1); Var psi = 1 + SR^2/2; Cov(psi1, psi2) = rho + SR1 SR2 rho^2 / 2 (Isserlis: E[u1 u2] = rho, E[u1 u2^2] = 0, E[u1^2 u2^2] = 1 + 2 rho^2). Hence theta = Var(psi1 - psi2) = 2(1 - rho) + (SR1^2 + SR2^2)/2 - SR1 SR2 rho^2, the Corollary 5.2 formula (row 747). Monte Carlo with 4,000,000 draws for SR pairs (0.05,0.05), (0.1,0.3), (0.5,1.0) and rho in {-0.9,-0.5,0,0.5,0.9}: largest |MC - closed form| = 0.0035, consistent with MC error. Sign check (common SR in {0.05, 0.5, 1.3, 1.41}, rho in +-{0.1, 0.5, 0.99}): sign(theta - (V1+V2)) = -sign(rho) for every point. So Proposition 5.4's "undersized under positive correlation, oversized under negative" holds for SR^2 < 2. The limit (line 427) follows from Theorem 5.1, sqrt((T-1)/T) -> 1 and Slutsky's lemma, as the proof on lines 433-436 states; the proof's identity (V1+V2) - theta = rho(2 + SR^2 rho) (line 436) matches the derivation above. PASS.
